anchor: like a girl, a mere babe
title: Patroclus' tears: the fountain and the little girl
greek: ἠΰτε κούρη νηπίη (ēyte kourē nēpiē)
short: Book 16 opens with two similes for Patroclus' weeping: a dark spring running down a cliff, and a little girl clutching her mother's dress to be picked up.
body: The first simile, tears pouring 'even as a fountain of dark water' down a sheer rock, repeats the image used for Agamemnon's weeping at 9.14-15. The second is Achilles' own, spoken to his friend, and is one of the most domestic pictures in the poem: a little girl running beside her mother, tugging at her dress, holding her up and looking up through her tears until she is lifted. The teasing is affectionate, but the roles it sets up matter. Achilles casts himself as the mother, the one whose help is wanted, and Patroclus as the child who needs comforting. In fact Patroclus has come to rebuke him. The tender beginning of this book will be matched by Achilles' own violent grief when Patroclus dies (18.22-35), and by the many images of parents and children that run through the war poem. Leaf comments on the vivid perfect δεδάκρυσαι, 'art thou bathed in tears'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.7-10.
Homer, Iliad 9.14-15 (the same fountain simile for Agamemnon).
Homer, Iliad 16.2-11 (Greek text).

title: The poet addresses Patroclus
greek: προσέφης Πατρόκλεες ἱππεῦ (prosephēs Patroklees hippeu), 'you said, horseman Patroclus'
short: Eight times in this book the narrator turns from 'he' to 'you' and speaks to Patroclus directly, more than to any other character in the Iliad.
body: Homeric narrative is usually impersonal, so the switch into the second person (apostrophe) stands out. In the Iliad it is used most often for Patroclus (eight times, all in Book 16) and Menelaus (seven times across the poem), and only occasionally for others (Melanippus at 15.582, Apollo at 15.365, Achilles at 20.2). In the Odyssey it is used for the swineherd Eumaeus. It happens at key moments: as Patroclus asks for the armour (16.20), as he charges the Lycians (584), in the question 'whom first, whom last didst thou slay, Patroclus, when the gods called thee deathward?' (692-3), and at his death (787, 812, 843). Some modern scholars stress that the vocative form simply fits the end of the hexameter line, while others, notably Elizabeth Block, read these addresses as a sign of affection and pathos. Both may be true. Murray's 'knight' translates hippeus, 'horseman' or 'charioteer'. Virgil imitated the device for Camilla (Aeneid 11.664-5).

sources.cite: Elizabeth Block, 'The Narrator Speaks: Apostrophe in Homer and Vergil', Transactions of the American Philological Association 112 (1982), 7-22.

Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.692-7 (Virgil's 'quem telo primum, quem postremum'; apostrophe and narrative) and on 17.681 (apostrophe).
Homer, Iliad 16.692-3 (Greek text).

title: 'The grey sea bore you'
greek: γλαυκὴ δέ σε τίκτε θάλασσα πέτραι τ' ἠλίβατοι (glaukē de se tikte thalassa petrai t' ēlibatoi)
short: Patroclus says Achilles is no son of Peleus and Thetis: the grey sea and the sheer cliffs bore him, so hard is his heart. The reproach was much imitated.
body: To accuse someone of being born from rocks or wild beasts is to call him inhuman, unable to feel pity. Patroclus' version has a sharp edge, because Achilles' mother really is a sea-goddess: the insult is half literal. Leaf records the ancient note that this is the only place where Homer gives the sea the epithet glaukē ('grey' or 'gleaming'), which suits the image of an unfeeling element. The same charge of a savage, unbending heart (here noos apēnēs) was made by Aias in the Embassy (9.628-32). The motif had a long afterlife. Catullus' Ariadne asks what lioness or sea-monster bore Theseus (64.154-7), and Virgil's Dido tells Aeneas that the rough Caucasus fathered him and Hyrcanian tigers nursed him (Aeneid 4.365-7). The Myrmidons make the same charge at 16.203: 'surely it was on gall that thy mother reared thee'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.34 (γλαυκή only here as epithet of the sea).
Catullus 64.154-7.
Virgil, Aeneid 4.365-7.

title: The borrowed armour
greek: δὸς δέ μοι ὤμοιιν τὰ σὰ τεύχεα θωρηχθῆναι (dos de moi ōmoiin ta sa teuchea thōrēchthēnai)
short: Patroclus repeats Nestor's idea: if Achilles will not fight, let Patroclus wear his armour so the Trojans mistake him for Achilles.
body: Patroclus repeats almost word for word the plan Nestor gave him in Book 11 (Leaf notes 16.36-45 = 11.794-803). Even the guess that Achilles may be 'shunning some oracle' (theopropiē) comes from Nestor. Achilles denies any oracle (16.50-1), though he has told the embassy of his choice between two fates (9.410-16). He agrees to the plan but sets a strict limit: drive the Trojans from the ships and come back. The trick works briefly, when the Trojans think Achilles has returned (16.278-83). But the armour also brings disaster. Apollo knocks the helmet off Patroclus, Hector strips the armour and puts it on (17.125-31, 17.192-7), and Achilles must have new armour made by Hephaestus (Book 18). Following Bergk, Leaf argued that the change of armour was not part of the original story. He notes that it is announced in only some fifteen lines, half of them suspect and several borrowed from elsewhere, though most readers find it essential to the plot. The plan that is meant to protect Patroclus is the one that kills him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XVI (on the change of armour) and note on 16.36-45.
Homer, Iliad 11.794-803 (Nestor's plan).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. θεοπροπία (prophecy, oracle).

title: Nēpios: 'fool that he was'
greek: μέγα νήπιος (mega nēpios)
short: The narrator calls Patroclus nēpios, 'a fool', literally 'childish', because he is praying for his own death without knowing it.
body: Nēpios first means 'infant, one who cannot yet speak' (LSJ: Latin infans), and then 'childish, without forethought'. Homer's narrator uses it to show the gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows. Agamemnon is nēpios when he trusts the false dream (2.38), Asius when he drives at the wall (12.113), Andromache when she heats a bath for Hector, who is already dead (22.445). The word frames Patroclus' story. Here, as he begs for the armour, 'it was to be his own evil death and fate for which he prayed' (16.46-7). It comes again when, carried away, he forgets Achilles' warning (16.684-7). Hector also calls him nēpie as he boasts over his body (16.833). Leaf suspected 16.46-7 of being a late addition, but the comment is typical of how Homer foreshadows: the narrator sees the outcome, and the character does not.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. νήπιος (infant; childish, without forethought).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.46-7.
Homer, Iliad 2.38; 12.113; 22.445 (other uses of nēpios).

title: Metanastēs: 'a dishonoured migrant'
greek: ὡς εἴ τιν' ἀτίμητον μετανάστην (hōs ei tin' atimēton metanastēn)
short: Achilles says Agamemnon treated him like a metanastēs, a migrant without status or protection, the lowest social position he can imagine.
body: A metanastēs is 'one who has left his home, wanderer, migrant', and LSJ notes the word was 'commonly a term of reproach'. In a society where status depended on land, kin and honour (timē), a migrant without family to avenge him was atimētos, 'without value'. Achilles uses the same line in his reply to the embassy (9.648). Leaf argues that it refers to Achilles himself and not to Briseis, since taking a spear-won slave woman would be no outrage. He notes that some ancient editors read a feminine form, metanastin, which would make it refer to her. The complaint shows that Achilles' anger is about public status as much as about losing Briseis. Achilles then takes a first step towards letting go: 'these things will we let be, as past and done' (16.60), a phrase he repeats when he finally renounces his anger (18.112, 19.65).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. μετανάστης (migrant, 'commonly as a term of reproach', Il. 9.648).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.59-60.
Homer, Iliad 9.646-8.

title: 'To loose the sacred veil of Troy'
greek: ὄφρ' οἶοι Τροίης ἱερὰ κρήδεμνα λύωμεν (ophr' oioi Troiēs hiera krēdemna lyōmen)
short: Achilles wishes every Greek and Trojan dead so that he and Patroclus alone might 'loosen Troy's sacred kredemna': its crown of walls, imagined as a woman's veil.
body: A krēdemnon is a woman's head-veil, and in the plural it is used figuratively for the battlements that crown a city (LSJ). Sacking a city is thus imagined as tearing the veil from a woman, and the image is darkened by what happened to captive women. It returns when Andromache throws off her krēdemnon on seeing Hector's body (22.468-72). The wish itself, that all others perish and the two friends alone take Troy, troubled ancient critics. The scholia report that Zenodotus suspected, and Aristarchus agreed, that the lines were inserted by people who believed Achilles and Patroclus were lovers. Leaf says modern critics reject them 'on less morbid grounds'. Homer never calls the two lovers. Later Greeks argued about it: Aeschylus' lost Myrmidons portrayed them as lovers, and the speaker Phaedrus in Plato's Symposium (180a) objects only to Aeschylus making Achilles the older partner.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. κρήδεμνον (veil; metaph. the battlements crowning a city's walls, Il. 16.100).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.97-100 (scholia on the athetesis) and 16.100.
Plato, Symposium 180a.

title: Invocation before the ship burns
greek: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχουσαι (espete nyn moi Mousai Olympia dōmat' echousai)
short: The poet calls on the Muses before telling how fire first fell on the Greek ships: the moment Zeus has been waiting for since Book 1.
body: Apart from the proem, the Iliad's narrator invokes the Muses only at important points: before the Catalogue of Ships (2.484-93), before Agamemnon's first victim (11.218-20), at the turn of the battle in 14.508-10, and here. Leaf says this appeal 'fitly introduces the great crisis of the Iliad', the lowest point of the Greeks, on which the plot turns. Hector cuts off the head of Aias' spear, and Aias recognises 'the deeds of the gods' and gives way. Fire then catches the stern of Protesilaus' ship, the sign Zeus has been waiting for (15.596-602). At once Achilles slaps his thighs and sends Patroclus out. The invocation therefore marks the hinge of the poem. Thetis' prayer is fulfilled, and the cost of that fulfilment, Patroclus' death, begins.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.112.
Homer, Iliad 2.484-93; 11.218-20; 14.508-10 (other invocations).
Homer, Iliad 16.112-24 (Greek text).

title: The Pelian ash spear
greek: Πηλιάδα μελίην, τὴν πατρὶ φίλῳ πόρε Χείρων (Pēliada meliēn, tēn patri philōi pore Cheirōn)
short: Patroclus puts on all of Achilles' armour except the great ash spear from Mount Pelion, which only Achilles can wield.
body: The arming scene follows the standard order (greaves, corselet, sword, shield, helmet, spears), but one piece is left out. The 'heavy and huge and strong' spear of ash wood from Mount Pelion was given to Peleus by the centaur Cheiron, Achilles' tutor, to be 'for the slaying of warriors'. No other Achaean can handle it. Leaf points out the wordplay between pēlai ('to wield'), Pelion and Peleus. He also notes an older tradition in the epic Cypria, in which Cheiron gave only the shaft. What Patroclus leaves behind matters. He can wear Achilles' armour and look like him, but he cannot do what Achilles does. The spear stays with Achilles and comes back into the story at its climax, when Achilles brandishes it against Hector (22.133-4) and kills him with it (22.317-27). The same lines are repeated when Achilles arms in Book 19 (19.388-91).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.143 (play on πῆλαι / Pelion; the Cypria).

title: Xanthus, Balius and the Harpy Podarge; Pedasus
greek: τοὺς ἔτεκε Ζεφύρῳ ἀνέμῳ Ἅρπυια Ποδάργη (tous eteke Zephyrōi anemōi Harpyia Podargē)
short: Achilles' immortal horses were foaled by the Harpy Podarge ('Swift-foot') to the West Wind; beside them runs Pedasus, a mortal horse who keeps pace with them.
body: Xanthus ('Bay' or 'Golden') and Balius ('Dappled') were gifts of the gods to Peleus (16.381, 16.867), given at his wedding in later tradition. Their mother is a Harpy, which Leaf explains as a storm-gust, literally a 'snatcher', personified, and quite unlike the foul bird-women of the Aeneid. Her name Podargē means 'swift-footed' or 'white-footed', and their father is Zephyrus, the West Wind, so they are horses born of wind and speed. Compare Boreas siring horses for Erichthonius (20.223-9). In Book 19 Xanthus will speak and foretell Achilles' death (19.404-17). In the side-traces runs Pedasus, taken when Achilles sacked Eetion's city (Thebe, Andromache's home, 6.414-16), 'being but mortal' yet keeping up with immortal horses. Like Patroclus beside Achilles, he is a mortal next to the more-than-mortal, and he dies first: Sarpedon's spear kills him (16.467-9).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.150 (the Harpy as storm-gust) and 16.152-3.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. Ἅρπυια.

title: Catalogue of the Myrmidons
greek: πεντήκοντ' ἦσαν νῆες θοαί (pentēkont' ēsan nēes thoai)
short: A short catalogue lists Achilles' fifty ships and five commanders, two of them sons of gods, before the Myrmidons enter the war.
body: Achilles brought fifty ships (as in the Catalogue of Ships, 2.685) with fifty men in each. His five commanders are: Menesthius, son of the river Spercheius and Peleus' daughter Polydora, though officially of Borus; Eudorus, son of Hermes and Polymele, a dancer in Artemis' chorus; Peisander, the best spearman after Patroclus; the old horseman Phoenix of Book 9; and Alcimedon. Spercheius is the river of Achilles' homeland, to which Peleus vowed his son's hair if he came home, a vow Achilles will break by cutting it for Patroclus (23.140-51). Homer calls it diipetēs, 'fallen from Zeus', that is, fed by rain. Leaf thought the catalogue a late addition, pointing out that Menesthius, Eudorus and Peisander are never mentioned again. Its purpose is to make Achilles' absent army fully present, with its own gods, mothers and stories, just before it marches out.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.168, 16.168-211 and 16.174-5.
Homer, Iliad 2.681-94 (Achilles' contingent); 23.140-51 (the hair vowed to Spercheius).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. διιπετής (fallen from Zeus, i.e. from heaven).

title: Argeiphontes (Hermes)
greek: κρατὺς Ἀργεϊφόντης (kratys Argeiphontēs)
short: A standing epithet of Hermes, traditionally 'Slayer of Argus', the hundred-eyed giant who guarded Io, though its true meaning was already disputed in antiquity.
body: In Homer Argeiphontēs is used of Hermes alone, often as a substitute for his name, as here, where the god who secretly fathers Eudorus is named only later as 'Hermes the helper'. LSJ gives the usual explanation, 'slayer of Argus': Hermes killed Argus, the many-eyed watchman Hera set over Io (Apollodorus 2.1.3; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.668-721). But the Iliad never tells that story, and ancient grammarians offered other explanations. LSJ records a derivation from argēs, 'serpent', giving 'serpent-slayer', and some took the first part from argos, 'bright' or 'swift'. Modern scholars also disagree, and the epithet may be older than the myth that came to explain it. In this episode Hermes appears in a typical role, as god of secret love affairs and of luck: he sees Polymele dancing for Artemis and visits her 'secretly' in her upper room.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. Ἀργειφόντης ('slayer of Argus'; 'variously explained by grammarians'; serpent-slayer).
Apollodorus, Library 2.1.3 (Hermes kills Argus).
Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.668-721.

title: Achilles' cup and libation
greek: ἐκάθηρε θεείῳ πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δ' ἔνιψ' ὕδατος (ekathēre theeiōi prōton, epeita d' enips' hydatos)
short: Achilles purifies a special cup kept for Zeus alone, washes his hands, and pours wine as he prays: a careful example of Homeric ritual.
body: The ritual is described step by step. From the chest Thetis packed for him, Achilles takes a cup from which no one else drinks and with which he pours libations only to Zeus. He purifies it with sulphur, rinses it with water, washes his own hands, draws wine, and prays standing in the middle of the courtyard (herkos), looking up to the sky. Leaf notes that the disinfecting power of sulphur fumes was known, and that the smell of a lightning-strike gave sulphur (theeion) a divine association, helped by a popular link with theos, 'god'. Odysseus fumigates his hall with sulphur after killing the suitors (Od. 22.481-94). Washing the hands before prayer is standard (compare 6.266-8, 24.302-5). The care Achilles takes adds to the irony of what follows: everything is done correctly, and Zeus still grants only half the prayer.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.228 (θέειον, sulphur) and 16.231 (the courtyard altar).
Homer, Odyssey 22.481-94 (Odysseus purifies the hall with sulphur).
Homer, Iliad 24.302-5 (washing hands before libation).

title: Zeus of Dodona, the Pelasgian
greek: Ζεῦ ἄνα Δωδωναῖε Πελασγικὲ τηλόθι ναίων (Zeu ana Dōdōnaie Pelasgike tēlothi naiōn)
short: Achilles prays to Zeus of Dodona in Epirus, the oldest Greek oracle, calling him 'Pelasgian', that is, belonging to the pre-Greek past.
body: Dodona, in the mountains of Epirus ('wintry Dodona'), was the seat of an oracle of Zeus who spoke through the rustling of a sacred oak (Od. 14.327-8, 19.296-7). Herodotus heard that it was the oldest oracle in Greece and tells stories of its founding by doves (2.52-7). 'Pelasgian' refers to the Pelasgians, whom the Greeks imagined as the earlier inhabitants of their land. The scholia say the shrine was founded by them. Why does Achilles of Phthia pray to a distant god in Epirus? Leaf suggests that Thessalian tribes, of whom Achilles' people were one, carried the cult with them from Epirus as they moved east, and that the Achaean tribes had taken over a prehistoric god at Dodona and identified him with their own Zeus. 'Dwelling afar' (tēlothi naiōn) expresses this distance. Compare 'Pelasgian Argos', the Thessalian plain of Achilles' contingent (2.681).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.233-5 (Dodona, the Pelasgians, Thessaly and Epirus).
Herodotus 2.52-7 (Dodona, the Pelasgians and the oracle).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. Πελασγικός.
Homer, Odyssey 14.327-8 (Zeus' oak at Dodona).

title: The Selli, priests of Dodona
greek: Σελλοὶ ... ὑποφῆται ἀνιπτόποδες χαμαιεῦναι (Selloi ... hypophētai aniptopodes chamaieunai)
short: Zeus' 'interpreters' at Dodona, the Selli, never wash their feet and sleep on the bare ground: ritual rules of an archaic priesthood.
body: The Selli are Zeus' hypophētai, 'interpreters' or 'spokesmen' of the god's will (LSJ), the men who put the oracle into words. Two ritual rules mark them out. They are aniptopodes, 'with unwashen feet', and chamaieunai, 'sleeping on the ground'. Sophocles remembers 'the mountain Selli who sleep on the ground' (Trachiniae 1166-7), and Euripides (fr. 367) has them neither washing their feet nor sleeping on beds. A common modern interpretation is that both rules keep the priests in contact with the earth from which the oracle's power came, but the Homeric text gives no reason. The name itself was disputed. Aristarchus read Selloi, while Pindar, according to Strabo, called them Helloi. Aristotle placed the original Hellas around Dodona, where 'the Selli' lived, and some ancient readers therefore connected the name with 'Hellenes'. Leaf thinks the question 'very evenly balanced'.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.vv. Σελλοί, ἀνιπτόπους, χαμαιεύνης, ὑποφήτης (citing Soph. Tr. 1167, Eur. fr. 367, Arist. Mete. 352b2, Strabo 7.7.10).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.234 (Σελλοί or Ἑλλοί; Strabo vii. 328; Pindar).
Sophocles, Trachiniae 1166-7.

anchor: a part the Father granted him
title: A prayer half granted
greek: τῷ δ' ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατήρ, ἕτερον δ' ἀνένευσε (tōi d' heteron men edōke patēr, heteron d' aneneuse)
short: Zeus grants that Patroclus will drive the Trojans from the ships, but refuses that he will come back safe. The narrator tells us at once.
body: Achilles asked for two things: glory for Patroclus, and his safe return with his armour and men. Zeus 'heard him', and the narrator immediately divides the answer: the first is granted, the second is denied (literally, Zeus 'nodded up', the Greek gesture of refusal). The audience therefore watches the whole of Patroclus' triumph knowing how it will end. The prayer also recalls the earlier one Achilles mentions: 'Aforetime verily thou didst hear my word ... and didst mightily smite the host of the Achaeans' (16.236-7). That fulfilled request, made through Thetis in Book 1, is the cause of this disaster. Virgil adapted the half-granted prayer when Apollo grants Arruns the death of Camilla but not his safe return home (Aeneid 11.794-5). In the Iliad prayer is a real exchange with the gods, but the gods answer it on their own terms.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.249-52 (variants) and apparatus.
Virgil, Aeneid 11.794-8 (Apollo grants half of Arruns' prayer).
Homer, Iliad 1.503-27 (the earlier prayer through Thetis).

title: The wasps' nest
greek: σφήκεσσιν ἐοικότες ... εἰνοδίοις (sphēkessin eoikotes ... einodiois)
short: The Myrmidons pour out like roadside wasps that boys have teased: the next traveller who passes is stung by the whole swarm.
body: Wasps that nest by the roadside (einodioi, LSJ) are a familiar country nuisance. Foolish boys keep poking at them, and the passing traveller then pays the price, as the whole swarm comes out 'in the valour of their hearts' to defend their young. Each part of the simile fits. The Myrmidons have been held back for days, irritated and taunted, as Achilles has just told them (16.200-9). Now they burst out together, and the Trojans, who happen to be there, take the sting. Homer used a wasp simile once before, for the Lapith defenders of the gate (12.167-70), but this one adds the cause of the anger and the innocent victim. Leaf records that some critics, including Hentze, have doubted the passage 259-77 because it delays the narrative and is made up largely of lines from elsewhere. Read as part of the scene, the simile captures the pent-up energy of an army finally released.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. σφήξ (wasp; 'called εἰνόδιοι, from their making their nests in the road, Il. 16.259').
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.259.
Homer, Iliad 12.167-70 (the earlier wasp simile).

title: Amisodarus, who reared the Chimaera
greek: υἷες ἀκοντισταὶ Ἀμισωδάρου, ὅς ῥα Χίμαιραν θρέψεν (huies akontistai Amisōdarou, hos rha Chimairan threpsen)
short: The Greek has Amisodarus ('Araisodarus' in this printing), a Lycian lord who reared the fire-breathing Chimaera that Bellerophon killed.
body: Murray's text here prints 'Araisodarus', but the Greek name is Amisōdaros. His sons Atymnius and Maris, comrades of Sarpedon, are killed by the brothers Antilochus and Thrasymedes, sons of Nestor, in a neat pairing of brothers against brothers. The Chimaera, a lion in front, a serpent behind and a goat in the middle, breathing fire, was killed by Bellerophon, Glaucus' grandfather, in Lycia (6.179-82). The detail ties these minor victims to Sarpedon's and Glaucus' Lycian world. Leaf observes that 'reared' (threpsen) makes the Chimaera sound like a domestic animal, and that Amisodaros is a genuine non-Greek name, comparable to Pixodaros of Caria (Herodotus 5.118). He refers to Plutarch's 'rationalizing history' of the man (Moralia 247F, in the Bravery of Women). The name is one of several small signs that the poet knew real Anatolian names.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.328 (Amisodaros a non-Greek name; Plutarch, Moralia 247F).
Homer, Iliad 6.179-82 (Bellerophon and the Chimaera).
Plutarch, Bravery of Women (Moralia 247F-248D), on the Lycians and Amisodarus.

title: Zeus' storm against crooked judgments
greek: οἳ βίῃ εἰν ἀγορῇ σκολιὰς κρίνωσι θέμιστας (hoi biēi ein agorēi skolias krinōsi themistas)
short: The Trojan horses' panic is compared to an autumn flood sent by Zeus in anger at men who give crooked judgments and drive out justice.
body: The simile's point of comparison is the roar of torrents and the galloping of the panic-stricken Trojan mares. But in the middle the poet explains why Zeus sends the storm: he is angry with men who 'by violence give crooked judgments in the place of gathering, and drive justice (dikē) out, recking not of the vengeance of the gods'. That is the language of Hesiod's Works and Days, where kings who take bribes give 'crooked judgments' and Zeus punishes the whole city (Works and Days 219-24, 238-47, 250-64). Leaf admired the simile but judged lines 387-88 spurious, a couplet made up out of Hesiodic phrases that is out of balance with the picture. Others reply that these lines are evidence that the idea of Zeus as guardian of justice was already part of the epic's world (compare the just king of Od. 19.109-14). Either way it is a rare moral comment from the Iliad's narrator.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.384 and 16.387-8.
Hesiod, Works and Days 219-24, 238-47, 250-64 (crooked judgments and Zeus' punishment).
Homer, Odyssey 19.109-14 (the just king).

title: The 'sacred fish'
greek: ἱερὸν ἰχθύν (hieron ichthyn)
short: Patroclus spears Thestor through the jaw and hauls him over the chariot rail like an angler landing a 'sacred fish' on line and hook.
body: This simile is grimly literal. The spear goes through Thestor's teeth like a hook through a fish's mouth, and Patroclus lands him 'agape'. Why the fish is called hieros, 'sacred', has long been debated. Leaf thought the epithet a survival from a time when eating fish was taboo: Homeric heroes eat fish only when they are starving (Od. 4.368-9), but the word that implied it was wrong to eat them remained. LSJ lists the phrase under animals regarded as taboo, with a cautious 'perhaps'. Later Greek used 'sacred fish' for a particular species, the anthias (Aristotle, History of Animals 620b35). Another possibility uses an older sense of hieros, 'strong' or 'lively', as in hieron menos, 'mighty strength'. Whichever is right, the image turns a hero into prey and shows Patroclus at his most savage.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.407 (the sacred fish and the dislike of eating fish).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἱερός ('of animals regarded as taboo ... so perh. ἱ. ἰχθύς Il. 16.407'; later = ἀνθίας).
Homer, Odyssey 4.368-9 (fishing from hunger).

title: Lycians 'without the mitrē'
greek: ἀμιτροχίτωνας ἑταίρους (amitrochitōnas hetairous)
short: Sarpedon's Lycians are amitrochitōnes, 'wearing no mitrē with the tunic': they lack the metal guard that Greek fighters wore at the waist.
body: The compound occurs only here in the Iliad. A mitrē in Homer is 'a piece of armour, apparently a metal guard worn round the waist' (LSJ), and it saves Menelaus from Pandarus' arrow (4.137, 4.187). Amitrochitōnes therefore means 'wearing the tunic without a mitrē'. Murray's 'ungirt' is a looser rendering. Leaf takes it to describe a Lycian national custom, one of the few places where Homer marks foreign dress, since in general 'the Greeks do not differ from their neighbours in dress'. The epithet comes at the moment Sarpedon sees his men falling and leaps down to face Patroclus with the bitter cry 'Shame, ye Lycians, whither do ye flee? Now be ye swift to fight'. Leaf discusses whether this is a command or a sarcastic remark. It begins the great duel of the book.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἀμιτροχίτωνες ('wearing no μίτρη with the χιτών, epith. of Lycian warriors, Il. 16.419').
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. μίτρα (metal guard worn round the waist, Il. 4.137).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.419 and 16.422.

anchor: twofold wise is my heart divided
title: Zeus, Sarpedon and fate
greek: διχθὰ δέ μοι κραδίη μέμονε φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντι (dichtha de moi kradiē memone phresin hormainonti)
short: Zeus considers rescuing his son Sarpedon from death; Hera warns him that the other gods will not approve, and he lets fate take its course.
body: This is the Iliad's most direct treatment of the relation between Zeus and fate (moira). Sarpedon is 'dearest of men' to him, but it is 'fated' (moir') that he die by Patroclus. Zeus wonders whether to snatch him away to Lycia. Hera answers that a mortal 'doomed long since by fate' should not be rescued. 'Do as thou wilt, but we other gods assent not', for every god has sons at Troy. The same exchange is repeated over Hector (22.168-85, with 22.181 = 16.443). Scholars disagree whether Zeus could actually override fate or whether the scene shows that his will and fate coincide. What the poem stresses is that he chooses not to. His grief appears in bloody raindrops shed on the earth to honour his son, a portent of slaughter (compare 11.53-5). Plato objected to a god lamenting in this way (Republic 388c-d). Zenodotus removed the whole dialogue, but Leaf calls the rescue of the body 'indispensable'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.431-2 (Zenodotus' excision), 16.459 (the bloody rain) and 16.666.
Homer, Iliad 22.168-85 (the parallel scene over Hector).
Plato, Republic 388c-d (criticises Il. 16.433-4).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ψιάς (drop; Il. 16.459).

title: Sleep and Death carry Sarpedon home
greek: θάνατόν τε ... καὶ νήδυμον ὕπνον (thanaton te ... kai nēdymon hypnon); Ὕπνῳ καὶ Θανάτῳ διδυμάοσιν (Hypnōi kai Thanatōi didymaosin)
short: Hera proposes, and Zeus orders, that the twin brothers Sleep and Death carry Sarpedon's body home to Lycia, after Apollo has washed and anointed it.
body: Hypnos and Thanatos are 'twin brothers' (16.672), children of Night in Hesiod (Theog. 211-12, 756-66), where Sleep is gentle and Death has an iron heart. Leaf calls their brotherhood 'a familiar allegory in all literature'. Sleep was a character in Book 14, where he helped Hera put Zeus to sleep. Here the brothers form a funeral escort. Apollo takes the body out of the fighting, washes it in the river, anoints it with ambrosia, dresses it in immortal clothing and gives it to the swift twins to carry to Lycia. The scene became one of the best-known subjects of Greek art. The Euphronios krater, an Attic red-figure vase of about 515 BC that the Metropolitan Museum of Art returned to Italy in 2008, shows winged Sleep and Death lifting Sarpedon's bleeding body while Hermes watches. In the Iliad's harsh world of unburied corpses, this is the one body rescued by the gods.

sources.cite: Hesiod, Theogony 211-12, 756-66 (Sleep and Death, children of Night).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.231 (the brotherhood of Sleep and Death).
Homer, Iliad 16.666-83 (Greek text).

title: 'Mound and pillar': the honour of the dead
greek: ταρχύσουσι ... τύμβῳ τε στήλῃ τε· τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων (tarchysousi ... tymbōi te stēlēi te; to gar geras esti thanontōn)
short: Sarpedon's kin will bury him 'with mound and pillar, for this is the due of the dead': the standard Homeric grave, an earth barrow with a standing stone.
body: The Homeric hero's grave is a tymbos (earth mound or barrow) topped with a stēlē (upright stone marker), as LSJ notes for both words. Ilus' grave-mound with its stele is a landmark on the Trojan plain (11.371), and Elpenor asks for a mound with his oar planted on it (Od. 11.74-8). Burial is a geras, 'the due' or privilege owed to the dead, the same word used of a warrior's prize of honour. The verb tarchyousi, 'will bury with honours', is rare. LSJ glosses the verb simply as 'bury solemnly', and its origin is uncertain. Sarpedon's honoured burial contrasts sharply with the threats to leave bodies for dogs that run through Books 15-24.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.vv. τύμβος, στήλη (gravestone, Il. 16.457), ταρχύω ('bury solemnly').
Homer, Iliad 11.371; Odyssey 11.74-8.

anchor: he fell as an oak falls
title: Sarpedon falls like a tree
greek: ἤριπε δ' ὡς ὅτε τις δρῦς ἤριπεν ἢ ἀχερωῒς ἠὲ πίτυς βλωθρή (ēripe d' hōs hote tis drys ēripen ē acherōis ēe pitys blōthrē)
short: Sarpedon falls like an oak, poplar or pine cut down by shipwrights for timber, then dies groaning like a bull under a lion.
body: The tree simile repeats exactly the lines used for the death of Asius (13.389-93), but it fits Sarpedon especially well. The tree is felled by shipwrights 'to be a ship's timber', and the battle is being fought for the ships, while Sarpedon was the first man over the Greek wall (16.558). He then lies 'clutching at the bloody dust', and a second simile follows: a bull, 'tawny and high of heart', groaning under a lion's jaws. Some critics suspected that two similes in a row meant one had been interpolated. Leaf answers that they describe different moments, first the fall and then the death-struggle on the ground. Sarpedon is the greatest warrior Patroclus kills and the only son of Zeus to die in the poem, and the double simile gives his death the weight that this demands.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.482-9 (the two similes describe different moments).
Homer, Iliad 13.389-93 (the same simile for Asius).

title: Sarpedon's last words to Glaucus
greek: Γλαῦκε πέπον πολεμιστὰ μετ' ἀνδράσι (Glauke pepon polemista met' andrasi)
short: Dying, Sarpedon charges his cousin Glaucus to rally the Lycians and save his armour from being stripped: shame would hang over Glaucus for ever.
body: Sarpedon and Glaucus are cousins, both grandsons of Bellerophon (6.196-206). In Book 12 Sarpedon gave Glaucus the Iliad's clearest statement of the heroic code (12.310-28). Kings are honoured with the best seats, meat and land, so they must fight in the front rank. And since death comes to everyone, it is better to win glory than to hold back. His last words put that code into practice. Glaucus must be a true 'warrior amid men' (Leaf: polemista used 'as a word of honour'), and if the Achaeans strip Sarpedon's armour, the shame will fall on Glaucus 'all thy days continually'. Patroclus then pulls out his spear, and the midriff follows it, so that he draws out 'the spear-point and the soul of Sarpedon' together. Glaucus, wounded by Teucer (12.387-9), can only pray to Apollo for help.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.492.
Homer, Iliad 12.310-28 (Sarpedon's speech to Glaucus).
Homer, Iliad 6.196-206 (the family of Bellerophon).

title: Apollo, the Lycian god
greek: κλῦθι ἄναξ ὅς που Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμῳ εἲς ἢ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ (klythi anax hos pou Lykiēs en pioni dēmōi eis ē eni Troiēi)
short: Glaucus prays to Apollo 'whether in Lycia or in Troy', since Apollo had strong cult links with Lycia; the god heals his wound at once.
body: The prayer uses a standard formula of uncertainty about where the god is ('haply here or haply there'), but the alternatives chosen are meaningful. Apollo was closely tied to Lycia. Homer calls him Lykēgenēs (4.101, 119), usually explained as 'Lycian-born', at Patara (LSJ), though some have explained it as 'born of light'. Herodotus mentions his oracle at Patara (1.182). For the Lycian Glaucus, Apollo is a home god as well as Troy's protector. The prayer is answered at once. Apollo stops the pain and the bleeding and puts strength into his heart, the god of plague in Book 1 now acting as a healer. Glaucus then goes to Hector with a bitter reproach, 'thou art utterly forgetful of the allies', which brings out the old tension between the Trojans and the allies who die far from home for them (compare 5.471-92, 17.142-68).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. Λυκηγενής ('commonly expld. Lycian-born, i.e. at Patara, Il. 4.101, 119').
Herodotus 1.182 (Apollo's oracle at Patara in Lycia).
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.514-16.

title: The sacred scales of Zeus
greek: γνῶ γὰρ Διὸς ἱρὰ τάλαντα (gnō gar Dios hira talanta)
short: Hector panics because 'he knew the turning of the sacred scales of Zeus': he sees that the god's balance has tipped against Troy.
body: Twice in the Iliad Zeus literally weighs fates on golden scales: the lots of Trojans and Achaeans at noon in Book 8 (8.69-74), and the deaths of Achilles and Hector in Book 22 (22.209-13), when Hector's sinks and Apollo leaves him. Odysseus also speaks of Zeus tilting his scales in war (Iliad 19.223-4). Here no weighing is described. Hector simply feels which way the battle is moving. Leaf comments that the word talanta 'practically means little more than will', the movement of battle reflecting the shifts in Zeus' purpose, like a balance swinging up and down. The image suits Book 16 well, since Zeus is constantly deciding (16.644-55), and Hector's flight leaves Sarpedon's body to be stripped. The idea later inspired Aeschylus' lost play Psychostasia ('Weighing of Souls') and Milton's golden scales in Paradise Lost (4.996-1004).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.658 (τάλαντα = will; the swinging balance).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. τάλαντον (balance, scales).

title: 'Three times ... but the fourth time'
greek: τρὶς μὲν ... ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος (tris men ... all' hote dē to tetarton epessyto daimoni isos)
short: Three times Patroclus climbs Troy's wall and three times Apollo pushes him back. The fourth time, 'like a god', he meets a warning, and later his death.
body: This is a fixed pattern in Homer for a hero who goes beyond mortal limits. Diomedes charges Apollo three times, and the fourth time the god shouts at him to remember that gods and men are not equal (5.436-44). Achilles lunges three times at the mist that hides Hector (20.445-8). Patroclus has the pattern twice. On the wall Apollo strikes his shining shield and warns: 'It is not fated ... that by thy spear the city of the lordly Trojans shall be laid waste, nay, nor by that of Achilles'. Later, when he 'thrice slew nine men' and charges a fourth time 'like a god' (daimoni isos), 'the end of life' appears. Leaf notes how closely 16.702-6 follows the Diomedes passage and calls the second sequence 'a fine climax in preparation for the catastrophe'. The phrase 'like a god' marks the point where Patroclus forgets that he is mortal.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.698-711 (parallels with 5.436-44) and 16.784-6.

title: Patroclus mocks Cebriones the 'diver'
greek: ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικώς ... ὡς ῥεῖα κυβιστᾷ (arneutēri eoikōs ... hōs rheia kybistāi)
short: Hector's charioteer Cebriones, struck by Patroclus' stone, pitches from the car 'like a diver'; Patroclus jokes that he would be a fine oyster-diver.
body: Cebriones is Priam's illegitimate son and Hector's driver. Patroclus' stone crushes his forehead and knocks out his eyes, and he falls headfirst. The word arneutēr can mean an acrobat or a diver (LSJ), and Patroclus picks up the image in the poem's cruellest joke: such an agile man, 'leaping from his ship were the sea never so stormy', could feed many people diving for tēthea. That word occurs only here in Homer. 'Oysters' is the usual translation, and LSJ connects it with a sea-squirt that Aristotle names. 'Verily among the Trojans too there be men that dive'. Leaf suggests the verb kybistan may mean tumbling as well as diving. The taunt shows how far battle has changed Patroclus, who tended Eurypylus' wound and whom Menelaus will remember as gentle to all (17.670-1). It also leads straight to the fight over Cebriones' body, in which Hector and Patroclus meet at last.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.vv. ἀρνευτήρ, κυβιστητήρ ('diver, Il. 16.750'), τήθυον.
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.742-50.

title: 'Mighty in his mightiness'
greek: κεῖτο μέγας μεγαλωστί, λελασμένος ἱπποσυνάων (keito megas megalōsti, lelasmenos hipposynaōn)
short: Cebriones lies in the whirling dust, 'huge in his hugeness, forgetful of his horsemanship': one of Homer's great lines for a dead warrior.
body: The phrase megas megalōsti doubles the idea of size. Leaf calls it an 'emphatic reduplication', comparable to 'alone in his aloneness'. It is used only three times. It describes Cebriones here, Achilles lying in the dust in grief for Patroclus (18.26-7), and the corpse of Achilles himself, fought over at Troy, in the Odyssey's underworld, where the full line is repeated: 'you lay in the whirl of dust, mighty in your mightiness, forgetful of your horsemanship' (Od. 24.39-40). The minor charioteer's death thus anticipates the death of the greatest hero. 'Forgetful of his horsemanship' is understated and moving, since the skill that defined him no longer matters. The next lines give a rare time-marker. The fighting lasts while the sun bestrides mid-heaven, until it turns towards 'the unyoking of oxen' (boulytonde, 16.779), the late afternoon, when the Greeks prevail 'beyond their portion'.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.776 (μέγας μεγαλωστί; also 18.26).
Homer, Odyssey 24.39-40 (the line used of Achilles' corpse).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. βουλυτός (time for unyoking oxen; Il. 16.779, Od. 9.58).

title: Apollo disarms Patroclus
greek: ἤντετο γάρ τοι Φοῖβος ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ δεινός (ēnteto gar toi Phoibos eni kraterēi hysminēi deinos)
short: Hidden in mist, Apollo strikes Patroclus' back with the flat of his hand; Achilles' helmet rolls in the dust, the armour falls away, and Patroclus stands stunned.
body: The god's attack is told with unusual slowness, and the narrator speaks to the victim directly: 'then for thee, Patroclus, did the end of life appear'. Leaf notes the powerful placing of deinos, 'an awful god', at the start of a line. Apollo, unseen in thick mist, stands behind him and strikes his back and shoulders with the flat of his hand, and his eyes spin. Then the god takes the armour off him piece by piece. The helmet that 'had not been suffered' to be soiled while it guarded Achilles' head rolls under the horses' hooves. The spear breaks, the shield and baldric fall, the corselet is loosened. This reverses the arming scene of 16.130-44. Leaf glosses the atē that seizes Patroclus as 'stupor', a physical meaning older than its later sense of moral blindness. The narrator adds that Zeus now gives the helmet to Hector, 'yet was destruction near at hand for him', since the armour will mark Hector for death in turn (22.322-5).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.784-9 and 16.805 (ἄτη = stupor).
Homer, Iliad 16.787-806 (Greek text).
Homer, Iliad 22.322-5 (Achilles finds the gap in his old armour on Hector).

title: Euphorbus, son of Panthous
greek: Πανθοΐδης Εὔφορβος (Panthoïdēs Euphorbos)
short: A young Trojan, Euphorbus, gives Patroclus the first spear-wound in the back, then runs. Much later, Pythagoras claimed to be Euphorbus reborn.
body: Euphorbus, son of Panthous and brother of Polydamas, is presented as an outstanding young man who surpassed those his own age in spear, horsemanship and speed, and who had knocked twenty men from their chariots in his first battle. Yet his part is unheroic. He strikes the disarmed Patroclus from behind and flees into the crowd 'unarmed though he was'. Menelaus kills him over Patroclus' body in the next book (17.43-60), in a famous simile of a young olive tree uprooted by a storm. Euphorbus had a remarkable afterlife. Pythagoras claimed that in an earlier life he had been Euphorbus, and he is said to have recognised Euphorbus' shield dedicated at Argos (Diogenes Laertius 8.4-5; Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.160-4). Leaf points to Horace's 'Panthoides iterum Orco demissus', 'the son of Panthous, sent down to Orcus a second time' (Odes 1.28.10).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.808 (Euphorbus and Pythagoras; Horace, Odes 1.28.10).
Horace, Odes 1.28.9-11.
Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.160-4.
Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers 8.4-5 (Pythagoras' earlier lives).

title: 'You are the third': Patroclus' dying words
greek: ἀλλά με μοῖρ' ὀλοὴ καὶ Λητοῦς ἔκτανεν υἱός, ἀνδρῶν δ' Εὔφορβος· σὺ δέ με τρίτος ἐξεναρίζεις (alla me moir' oloē kai Lētous ektanen huios, andrōn d' Euphorbos; sy de me tritos exenarizeis)
short: Patroclus tells the boasting Hector that Fate and Apollo killed him, then Euphorbus; Hector is only third, and Achilles will soon kill him in turn.
body: Hector's victory speech is full of mistaken confidence: he imagines Achilles told Patroclus to bring back Hector's bloody tunic. Patroclus deflates it. His death was Fate, working through Apollo (Leaf notes the singular verb, making the two 'a sort of hendiadys': 'fate by the hand of Apollo'), and then Euphorbus. 'Thou art the third in my slaying', Hector merely finishing off a disarmed, wounded man. If twenty men like Hector had faced him, he says, they would all have died. Then comes the prophecy: death and 'mighty fate' stand close beside Hector, who will die at Achilles' hands. That dying men can see the future was a common ancient belief. The scholia cite Artemon, and Leaf adds Socrates in Plato's Apology (39c) and Cicero (On Divination 1.63-4). Hector's own dying words will likewise foretell Achilles' death at the hands of Paris and Apollo (22.355-60).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 16.849-50 (fate and Apollo as hendiadys) and 16.851-4 (prophecy of the dying; Plato, Apology 39c; Cicero, Div. 1.63).
Plato, Apology 39c.
Homer, Iliad 22.355-60 (Hector's dying prophecy).

title: The soul's departure
greek: ψυχὴ δ' ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη Ἄϊδος δὲ βεβήκει, ὃν πότμον γοόωσα, λιποῦσ' ἀνδροτῆτα καὶ ἥβην (psychē d' ek rhetheōn ptamenē Aïdos de bebēkei, hon potmon goōsa, lipous' androtēta kai hēbēn)
short: Patroclus' psychē flies from his limbs to Hades, 'bewailing her fate, leaving manliness and youth'. The same lines are used only once more, for Hector's death.
body: In Homer the psychē is the life-breath that leaves the body at death and goes to Hades as a shade. It is not the seat of thought or feeling in life. These three lines are used only twice in the poem, for Patroclus and, word for word, for Hector, so their deaths answer each other. Androtēs means 'manhood' (LSJ). Aristarchus insisted it means a man's human nature and not 'courage'. The form is unusual, and variants ἀδροτῆτα and ἁδροτῆτα are recorded, but Leaf rejects the conjectures and concludes that we have no choice but to acquiesce in the ordinary reading. Even after death Hector keeps speaking to the corpse, refusing to accept the prophecy he has just heard.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 16.857 (ἀνδροτῆτα: variants and Aristarchus).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. ἀνδροτής ('manhood', Il. 16.857, 24.6; vv.ll. ἀδρ-, ἁδρ-).
Homer, Iliad 22.361-3 (the same lines for Hector).
